implementation_notes: The pattern lands on one package call chain: a claims struct embedding jwt.RegisteredClaims carries iss, sub, aud, exp, iat and jti, jwt.NewWithClaims pairs it with jwt.SigningMethodRS256, the kid is set on Token.Header before signing, and Token.SignedString(*rsa.PrivateKey) is the signing authority. What replaces the classic structure: struct tags plus the signing method replace the builder class, and the consumer mirror is jwt.ParseWithClaims with parser options (jwt.WithIssuer, jwt.WithAudience, jwt.WithValidMethods, jwt.WithExpirationRequired) - note that signing and validation are separate calls, so a program that only signs has no validation unless it builds it. The library deliberately makes alg=none hard to reach (it requires jwt.UnsafeAllowNoneSignatureType as the key), which is RFC 8725 encoded as an API shape.
code_sketch:
claims := jwt.RegisteredClaims{
    Issuer:    "https://idp.example",
    Subject:   userID,
    Audience:  jwt.ClaimStrings{"https://api.example"},
    ExpiresAt: jwt.NewNumericDate(time.Now().Add(5 * time.Minute)),
    IssuedAt:  jwt.NewNumericDate(time.Now()),
    ID:        uuid.NewString(),
}
tok := jwt.NewWithClaims(jwt.SigningMethodRS256, claims)
tok.Header["kid"] = kid
signed, err := tok.SignedString(privateKey) // *rsa.PrivateKey
pitfalls: SignedString takes the concrete key type for the method (*rsa.PrivateKey for RS256, []byte for HS256): a wrong type is a runtime error, never a compile error.
RegisteredClaims uses pointer time values with omitempty semantics, so a nil ExpiresAt silently omits exp and mints a non-expiring assertion.
On the consumer side the alg header is attacker-controlled: pin allowed methods with jwt.WithValidMethods so an HS256 token is rejected before key selection.
Errors from token creation are easy to ignore because the token struct exists either way; branch on the error before the token is used anywhere.
